idiom_name: typed HttpClient client registered with AddHttpClient<T> (+ System.Net.Http.Json)
implementation_notes: The platform supplies both roles: HttpClient is the connection (connection pool, HTTP/2, redirect policy and handler pipeline configured once) and a typed client class is the gateway - it takes the HttpClient in its constructor and exposes domestic methods, so callers never touch HttpRequestMessage or JSON. System.Net.Http.Json's GetFromJsonAsync/PostAsJsonAsync do the payload translation (System.Text.Json), while failure translation stays explicit: call EnsureSuccessStatusCode or map the status code to your own exception, because HttpClient throws only for transport failures. Register the gateway with AddHttpClient<T> so a DelegatingHandler carries authentication, retry and telemetry, and so the HttpMessageHandler remains the documented substitution point in tests.
pitfalls: Creating a fresh HttpClient per call (or per gateway instance) defeats connection reuse and risks socket exhaustion and stale DNS; the documented guidance is one long-lived client or a factory-provided typed client.
Reusing the same HttpClient while mutating DefaultRequestHeaders per request is a thread-safety bug - configure auth and headers in handlers or per request instead.
A gateway that caches mutable state (token, cursor) stops being thread-safe because typed clients are registered transient per resolution; put shared state behind a thread-safe store or handler.

Under System.Text.Json the default options are strict about casing and fail on unknown members only when configured to; choose PropertyNameCaseInsensitive/JsonSerializerOptions deliberately, at the gateway.
